extracted.intended_audience: U.S. design patent applicants, patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and IP practitioners advising clients on international design protection
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for filing and prosecuting industrial/design registrations under the Hague Agreement (1999 Geneva Act) to obtain protection in multiple contracting states from a single international application. Covers procedural options, substantive requirements that vary by jurisdiction, strategic considerations, and post-registration effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of an international design application (up to 100 designs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An international application under the Hague Design Agreement affords an applicant the option of obtaining protection for up to 100 industrial designs in designated member countries and organizations by filing a single international application, in a single language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While up to 100 designs can be included in the international filing, recognize that many national systems (notably the U.S.) allow only one design per national design application; plan for divisional filings where necessary. Use the single-application scope to maximize worldwide coverage and cost-efficiency, but vet national limits before grouping designs together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route: WIPO International Bureau or national Office
rubrics_metrics.description: The international design application can be filed either directly with the International Bureau of WIPO, or through the national Office in the applicant's country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose filing route based on practitioner preference and local requirements—filing through the national Office is a common route for U.S. applicants and may streamline interaction with the USPTO; filing direct with WIPO is also an option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must comport with each designated jurisdiction’s substantive requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Although filed centrally, the international design application will, in due time, undergo an examination process in each designated country or region and thus must comport with each jurisdiction’s requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be familiar with substantive laws and regulations (e.g., novelty, formalities, drawing standards) in each designated contracting state before filing. The international system streamlines filing but does not override national substantive standards; noncompliance in a designated state can lead to refusal in that state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in drawing and depiction requirements across countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing requirements can widely vary from country to country; acceptable depictions in the international application (for example, photographs) may not meet national requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, although photographs may be accepted in some jurisdictions, the U.S. typically requires line drawings with specific depiction of edges and shading. Reconcile and prepare representations that meet the most restrictive relevant national standards or plan for national divisional filings to conform to local drawing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: National limitations on number of designs examinable (U.S. single-design rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: While an international application can contain up to 100 different designs, only one design is allowable for a national design application in the U.S. and thus only one design will typically be examined in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexamined designs in the international application may be pursued in the U.S. by filing divisional applications directly with the USPTO. Check similar limitations in other designated states and plan filing strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility restrictions related to contracting-state membership and applicant nationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain restrictions apply to various countries, and those restrictions attach to their citizens as applicants: Canada and China are not members of the Hague Design Agreement; design registration in non-member countries requires direct national filing. Applications that include citizens of non-contracting states as inventors cannot be filed under the Hague Design Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the citizenship/nationality of applicants/ inventors and the membership status of target countries before selecting the Hague route. If key jurisdictions are non-members or inventors are citizens of non-members, plan direct national or regional filings instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: International recording, publication timing, and publication deferment
rubrics_metrics.description: International designs filed with the International Bureau will be recorded in the International Register and published without substantive review or examination; publication of the designs occurs six months after the date of international registration, although publication may be deferred where permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand publication timing because copies are sent to each designated country or region; use available deferment options where strategic confidentiality or timing concerns exist (subject to whether the Hague Agreement and receiving states permit deferral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination and national outcomes (approval or refusal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive examination follows in each designated country, which can either approve or refuse registration of the design(s) in the same fashion as designs are examined in nationally filed applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect differing outcomes across jurisdictions; an international grant does not guarantee acceptance everywhere. Monitor national examinations and be prepared to respond to objections under each country's law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claims under the Paris Convention determined by national law
rubrics_metrics.description: The international design application may rely for priority on prior-filed applications under the Paris Convention, but such priority is determined depending on the laws of each designated state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming priority, check how each designated contracting state interprets and applies priority rights to international design applications to avoid unintended loss of priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal effect after registration equals national filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Following registration of the design, no difference exists in the legal force and effect of a registered design that originated under the Hague Design Agreement or from a national filing in each designated contracting country or region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the Hague system to obtain registrations that have the same legal force as domestically filed registrations in contracting states, and note ancillary benefits such as standardized formal requirements and a common patent term (noted as a standard 15 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic trade-offs: cost-effectiveness vs reconciling national requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing an avenue through which a design can be submitted to multiple countries simultaneously affords an applicant a simple and cost-effective tool for pursuing design protection in multiple jurisdictions; however, reconciling drawing requirements and national limitations may be a drawback for some applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the streamlined filing and possible cost savings against the administrative and substantive work needed to satisfy the most restrictive national requirements. For U.S. applicants who regularly seek design rights in non-member countries such as Canada and China, direct national or regional filings may be preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursuing unexamined designs via divisional filings in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexamined designs remaining in an international application may be pursued, at least in the U.S., by filing divisional applications directly with the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple designs were filed internationally but only one is examinable domestically, plan for timely divisional filings with the USPTO to secure examination for the remaining designs and to comply with U.S. formalities and drawing standards.
